chapter_theme: Under the heading நட்பில் விலக்கு, seven verses on the friends to be shunned: those once dear as the eye's pupil who turn to plotting one's life, those kept as a reserve who fail at need, the friend who withdraws to piety when the battle comes, the fools who heed slander, the shameless on whom love is wasted, the friend who breaks and must be broken with, and the double-dealer who will hold to neither side.

135.reading: Even those who befriended one with love as dear as the pupil of the eye may, when it comes to the reckoning, stand as strangers and go about scheming to take one's life, yet Death itself keeps a man until his allotted eating is done.
135.nuance: The proverb consoles rather than warns: the false friend's plot cannot cut a life short, because the term is Death's and not the plotter's. Death is pictured as an eater who also guards its food until the time of eating (உண்ணும் துணை), so the very power one fears is what protects one from the friend. எண்ணும் துணையில் in line 2 may also mean 'in the time it takes to think', making the friend's turn sudden.

pazhamozhi.literal: Death guards a man for as long as he is to eat

story.act: no story; Death keeps every life until its appointed portion is consumed

pazhamozhi.applied_to: a treacherous friend's plotting cannot take a life before its fated term

136.reading: Those one cherished as a store laid by for the day of weakness do not help with a single thing when trouble comes, the verse tells a woman with fresh bangles, and if they go about after setting one in the midst of danger, that is taking away the ladder after making one climb to the loft.
136.nuance: The fault grows across the verse: first the reserve friend merely fails to help, then he is the one who has put the man in peril and leaves him there, as the ladder is taken from one already raised. எயப்புழி stands for எய்ப்புழி, the time of exhaustion or want. அச்சிடை இட்டு is compressed; the reading takes அச்சு as அச்சம், danger, though it could be the axle or a frame, which would leave the image of being stranded unchanged.

pazhamozhi.literal: removing the ladder after making someone climb into the loft

story.act: no story; a man is helped up to a loft and the ladder is taken away

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the reserve friend who leads one into danger and then withdraws his help

137.reading: Those who, like the milk-white one with the man of the snake banner, do not join the battle and strike, but go off on the road and perform great penance for their friends, are those who lift a child onto their shoulders when the festival is over.
137.nuance: The verse scorns piety put in the place of a friend's duty: the penance may be done in the friend's name, but help that arrives after the need is past is the shoulder offered when the procession has gone. It names its figures only by epithet, the white-bodied one and the bearer of the snake flag.

pazhamozhi.literal: those who lift someone on their shoulders after the festival is over

story.act: the milk-white one did not fight in the battle for his friend of the snake banner but went away on the road doing penance
story.tradition: identified by tradition as Balarama, who left on pilgrimage rather than fight for Duryodhana in the Bharata war; the verse uses only the epithets

pazhamozhi.applied_to: a friend who withdraws to pious works when his friend needs him in battle gives help too late to be any

138.reading: The highest kind of men, even when they look into it, do not find that this friend has a rift with that one, but the lowest, because they take in the tale-bearing spoken to their face, show that the friendship of fools is painful afterwards.
138.nuance: The verse ranks friends by how they receive slander: the best do not credit a quarrel even when they search for one, the lowest believe what is told them in person. The pain of the fool's friendship comes later, when the slander has done its work. தெரிதலால் is read as 'heeding'; it could mean that the low are known by the slander they speak openly, which would make them the tale-bearers rather than the hearers.

pazhamozhi.literal: the friendship of fools turns painful afterwards

story.act: no story; the fool's friendship, sweet at first, pains in the end

pazhamozhi.applied_to: friends who believe slander against one break the bond and bring later pain

139.reading: When one has befriended people from the heart and treated them as one's own, what of it if they, having no shame within, do not behave well, the verse asks a deer-eyed woman: they will not care for one even by mistake, and the love is moonlight shed in the forest.
139.nuance: The proverb makes the loss one of waste rather than injury: moonlight falling in an empty forest harms no one and delights no one. The subject of மறந்தும் பரியலரா is not stated; it may be the shameless friends, who never care, or the wise, who do not grieve over such friends even in passing. On either reading the heart's friendship given to the shameless is spent for nothing.

pazhamozhi.literal: moonlight that falls in the forest

story.act: no story; moonlight spilt where no one sees it

pazhamozhi.applied_to: love given to shameless friends who do not return it is wasted

140.reading: Toward those who act without fellowship, unlike people who have seen and known one, the right course is to behave not as one who knew them of old but as they do, breaking off, drawing away and casting them out, for the remedy for one who breaks is to break.
140.nuance: The verse answers the claim of old acquaintance directly: பண்டறிவார் போலாது, 'not like one who knew them before', sets aside the indulgence long friendship usually earns. The proverb's மருந்து treats the break as a cure, not a revenge. கண்டறிவார் போலார் is compressed and may describe them as acting like strangers.

pazhamozhi.literal: for one who has broken away, breaking away is the medicine

story.act: no story; a cure matched to the ailment

pazhamozhi.applied_to: a friend who turns unfriendly is to be answered by ending the friendship, not by old indulgence

141.reading: Those who go both to their great friends and to the enemies, speak to each as if settled without wavering, and yet join firmly with neither are the ones people call a brand burning at both ends.
141.nuance: The fault is not open betrayal but refusal to belong: the double speaker seems resolved to each side, and the brand that burns at both ends cannot be held by either party. திரிவின்றித் தீர்ந்தார்போல், 'as if settled without change', marks the show of firmness.

pazhamozhi.literal: they are called a firebrand alight at both ends

story.act: no story; a stick burning at both ends that no one can grasp

pazhamozhi.applied_to: one who courts both friends and their enemies without committing to either

links.note: Naladiyar 110 says what was fixed at birth does not shrink or grow and so asks why grieve at ruin; Pazhamozhi 135 turns the same fixed term against a friend turned murderer, who cannot shorten it.
links.teaches: Together they show the fixed-term doctrine working in two directions: the Naladiyar uses it to quiet grief over loss, while Pazhamozhi uses it to quiet fear of betrayal, making fate a shelter against human malice.
links.list_adds: its proverb pictures Death as the guard of a life until its portion is eaten, so the fixed span becomes protection from a plotting friend rather than a reason for calm at ruin.

links.note: Both picture Death as an eater: Nanmanikkadigai 40 says it does not take its food at anyone's bidding, Pazhamozhi 135 that it guards a man until his eating is done.
links.teaches: Put together, Death's refusal to eat at command explains the Pazhamozhi consolation: no plotter can order Death to take a man early, so the same appetite that cannot be bribed cannot be hurried either.

links.note: Naladiyar 218 asks what use is a close friend who gives not even a fly's foot of help; Pazhamozhi 136 names the friend kept as a reserve who gives none at need and adds that he first set one in danger.
links.teaches: The pair separates two failures the word 'useless friend' joins: the Naladiyar's friend merely gives nothing, while Pazhamozhi's raises one into peril and then withdraws, so the worst friend is the one whose help began.
links.list_adds: the ladder proverb adds the stage the quatrain lacks, being helped up and then stranded, which makes a half-given help worse than none.

links.note: Kural 788 says friendship clears distress there and then, like the hand catching a slipping garment; Pazhamozhi 137 shows a friend who chose penance over battle, help offered when the festival is over.
links.teaches: Read with the Kural's 'there and then', the Balarama story shows that timing is the whole of friendship's help, so even a holy act done for the friend fails if it replaces help at the moment of need.
links.list_adds: it sets an epic case and a proverb of lateness against the couplet's simile of speed, and ranks the friend's present help above pious works done on his behalf.

links.note: Naladiyar 238 is a vow to put one's life in a distressed friend's hands; Pazhamozhi 137 condemns the friend who went off to penance instead of fighting beside his friend.
links.teaches: The vow and the story are the two halves of one rule: the Naladiyar says what the friend owes in the hour of danger, Pazhamozhi shows a famous figure who withheld it and calls his religion a late shoulder.
links.list_adds: it supplies a named failure for the quatrain's oath, so the duty to risk one's life is shown being broken by a pious withdrawal rather than by cowardice.

links.note: Kural 839 calls the friendship of fools very sweet because parting from them brings no pain; Pazhamozhi 138 closes with the proverb that the friendship of fools is painful afterwards. The tension holds if the Kural's line is read plainly rather than as irony.
links.teaches: The two place the pain of a fool's friendship differently: the Kural finds none at the parting because there was no real bond, while Pazhamozhi finds pain later because the fool believes slander and breaks the bond.
links.list_adds: it ranks friends by how they take slander, highest against lowest, and so names the cause of the later pain, which the couplet does not.

links.note: Naladiyar 189 says the pure in heart stay unshaken by cruel slander like a shielded flame; Pazhamozhi 138 makes the same steadiness the mark of the highest friend, who finds no rift even when looking, against the lowest, who believe.
links.teaches: The pair moves resistance to slander from a private virtue to a test of friendship: the Naladiyar's steady heart protects itself, Pazhamozhi's protects the bond between two other people.
links.list_adds: it sets the steady man against his opposite and names what the credulous one's belief costs, the friendship's later pain.

links.note: Naladiyar 229 says that when those taken as one's own prove otherwise, one should honour them all the more and keep it within; Pazhamozhi 139 calls heart's friendship given to the shameless moonlight shed in the forest.
links.teaches: Read together, the Naladiyar's counsel to keep honouring the false friend meets its limit in shamelessness: where the other has no shame within, the honour reaches no one, and Pazhamozhi counts it wasted.
links.list_adds: its proverb names the outcome the quatrain leaves out, that continued regard for the shameless lights an empty forest.

links.note: Kural 805 says that when friends do what hurts one should read it as folly or great intimacy; Pazhamozhi 140 says one should not act as one who knew them of old but break with them as they broke.
links.teaches: The two give opposite rules for the old friend who turns unfriendly: the Kural asks for a generous reading of the hurt, Pazhamozhi denies old acquaintance any claim and prescribes the break as a cure.
links.list_adds: its proverb treats breaking off as a medicine, so ending the friendship becomes a remedy rather than a failure of the patience the couplet asks.

links.note: Naladiyar 226 asks whether anyone cuts off his own hand because it poked his eye, so a friend who hurts should not be cast off; Pazhamozhi 140 says breaking with one who breaks is the remedy.
links.teaches: The images decide the rule: the Naladiyar makes the friend one's own limb, so cutting him off is self-harm, while Pazhamozhi makes the broken friendship an ailment, so the cut is the cure.
links.list_adds: the medicine proverb answers the quatrain's body image with one of cure, turning the same separation from mutilation into healing.

links.note: Naladiyar 375 uses the eel that shows one end to the snake and the other to the fish for women of double conduct; Pazhamozhi 141 calls the man who courts both friends and enemies a brand burning at both ends.
links.teaches: Both books picture double dealing as one body with two ends, but the eel profits by fitting each side, while the brand burns whoever holds it, so Pazhamozhi makes the two-sided man a danger to both sides rather than a clever survivor.
links.list_adds: it moves the two-ended image from the courtesan to the go-between among friends and foes, and its proverb names the harm to the holder that the eel image does not.

links.note: Pazhamozhi 139 counts love given to the shameless as wasted; 140 goes on to say what to do when a friend turns unfriendly: break with him.
links.teaches: Read in order, the two verses move from loss to action: once the love is seen to be moonlight in a forest, the next counsel is to stop shedding it and answer the break with a break.

source_issues: 137 line 1: the site's text lacks line 1 (பாப்புக் கொடியாற்குப் பால்மேனி யான்போலத்); the corpus keeps it and the reading depends on it.
136 line 1: எயப்புழி appears to stand for எய்ப்புழி.
136 line 3: அச்சிடை இட்டு is of doubtful sense (fear, or an axle or frame).
136, 138: the closing quotation includes a full stop inside the marks.
